item.title: Wisconsin fugitive wanted on child rape charges captured in Byhalia after pursuit - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
BYHALIA — A Wisconsin man wanted on two counts of child rape was taken into custody Thursday following a vehicle pursuit and manhunt that prompted a temporary school lockdown in the Byhalia area.

Authorities identified the suspect as Robert Gower, who is wanted in Sauk County, Wisconsin, on two counts of child rape.

According to officials, Gower was apprehended by the U.S. Marshals Service, along with deputies from Marshall and DeSoto counties and officers with Byhalia Police.

Investigators said Gower initially fled from law enforcement in a vehicle before abandoning it and running into a wooded area south of East Stonewall Road.

The incident led to a lockdown of nearby schools as a precaution while officers searched for the suspect. The lockdown has since been lifted.

Gower was taken into custody without incident and booked into the DeSoto County Jail as a fugitive from justice. He is also facing additional charges in Mississippi, including disorderly conduct, failure to obey and felony fleeing a law enforcement officer.

He is scheduled to appear in Hernando Circuit Court on the felony fleeing charge. Gower also has a June 26 court date in DeSoto County Circuit Court related to the additional charges.

Authorities said Sauk County is located near the Milwaukee area.

item.title: Sheriff: Realistic toy guns can lead to dangerous misunderstandings - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
DESOTO COUNTY – DeSoto County Sheriff Thomas Tuggle is urging parents to avoid buying toy guns that closely resemble real firearms, warning that they can create dangerous situations for children and law enforcement.

In a message to the community, Tuggle said realistic-looking toy guns can force deputies to make split-second decisions in situations where it may be impossible to tell whether a weapon is real.

“When a child is holding an object that looks indistinguishable from a real weapon, there’s no time to pause and verify if it’s a toy,” Tuggle said. “Such moments of uncertainty can lead to tragedy, and no parent, officer, or community should bear the burden of a preventable mistake.”

Tuggle said the warning is not about discouraging childhood play, but about making safer choices when it comes to toys that can easily be mistaken for actual firearms.

He encouraged parents to choose brightly colored toy guns that are easier to distinguish from real weapons and to talk with their children about safety, respect for law enforcement and the potential consequences of their actions.

“Our mission is to protect this community every day,” Tuggle said. “Help us keep your children safe through careful decisions that minimize their risk of harm.”

The sheriff’s message came alongside an image showing two handguns and challenging viewers to identify which one was a toy.

item.title: Pizza Shack offering free cheesy bread, gift card to support Rankin County Animal Shelter - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
BRANDON – Pizza Shack is encouraging the community to support the Rankin County Animal Shelter through a donation and pet adoption drive at its Brandon location.

In a social media post, The Cleaners by Pizza Shack said some animals at the shelter are still waiting for food, care and a home, and urged residents to help.

As part of the effort, customers who bring a donation for the shelter will receive a free Honey Fire Cheesy Bread, according to the post.

The business also said anyone who adopts a pet from the Rankin County Animal Shelter will receive a $100 Pizza Shack gift card.

Pizza Shack thanked Josh Jones of Thrivent for supporting the effort through Thrivent Action Team funds, which the business said is helping it give back to local animal shelters.

Pizza Shack is located at 237 W. Government St. in Brandon.

item.title: On International Day of Mastering Conversations That Matter, listening, not winning, can help bridge the divide - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
STATEWIDE — As we navigate deep political and cultural divisions, International Day of Mastering Conversations That Matter offers a timely reminder: progress often begins with a conversation, and the willingness to truly listen.

Observed each year on April 17, the day highlights the role meaningful, respectful dialogue has played throughout human history, from ancient debating societies in Greece and India to modern discussions that shape public policy, relationships and social change. According to NationalToday.com, the exchange of ideas, debated, refined and shared, has driven everything from scientific advancement to the rise and fall of civilizations.

But in today’s climate, many of those conversations are breaking down. Throw in the phenomenon that is the internet bully, and it’s almost a lost cause. But just ALMOST.

Psychologists say the problem is not actually disagreement, it’s avoidance. Research cited by the American Psychological Association shows people often steer clear of deeper discussions, especially with those who have opposing views, because they expect there to be some kind of discomfort or conflict. In reality, those conversations are frequently more rewarding and less awkward than anticipated.

“Conversation is this ancient technology for aligning our brains so that we can be on the same page,” said Thalia Wheatley, a Dartmouth College professor quoted by the APA. Yet despite the importance of just having a good talk, many Americans struggle to do effectively, particularly across ideological divides.

That divide is increasingly visible in everyday life, from political debates to family dinners, where conversations can quickly turn into arguments or shut down entirely. Experts say one key shift could help: moving from trying to “win” conversations to trying to understand them.

A meaningful conversation, according to the wellness app Calm’s research, isn’t defined by perfect wording but by presence and the ability to be open, curious and attentive. When people feel heard and understood, even briefly, it can strengthen relationships, reduce stress and build trust.

Studies show those interactions also have measurable mental health benefits. Deeper conversations can lower stress hormones, reduce feelings of loneliness and improve emotional resilience. They also activate parts of the brain associated with connection and reward, helping people feel more grounded and supported.

Still, meaningful dialogue requires effort, and sometimes discomfort.

The APA notes that disagreements are inevitable, but how they are handled determines whether relationships fracture or grow. Researchers have identified techniques that can make tough conversations more productive, including acknowledging the other person’s perspective, finding common ground and reframing statements to reduce defensiveness.

“In any conversation, no matter how much we disagree, we agree on something,” psychologist Julia Minson said in APA research.

That idea aligns with the purpose behind International Day of Mastering Conversations That Matter, which encourages people to engage, not retreat. Find the common ground and love each other on it.

The observance traces its roots to thousands of years of human dialogue. Early debating societies emerged as far back as 5000 B.C., while the Enlightenment era fostered intellectual exchange that shaped modern democratic thought. Today, educators still emphasize communication skills, recognizing that even the best ideas have little impact if they cannot be clearly expressed.

But mastering conversation is not just about speaking. You have to listen too.

Experts point to simple but effective habits like asking open-ended questions, reflecting what others say, paying attention to body language, and resisting the urge to interrupt or dismiss opposing views. Compassion is especially critical, the ability to consider where someone else is coming from, even when you disagree.

That approach may feel small or uncomfortable, but its impact can make all the difference.

In a time when national discourse often feels polarized and impersonal, meaningful conversations offer a way to reconnect, one interaction at a time. Whether it is a discussion with a neighbor, a coworker or a family member, choosing curiosity over confrontation can begin to close gaps that seem otherwise insurmountable.

The message behind the day is pretty clear: differences are not the problem, the inability to talk about them is. So try it. Talk to someone today who doesn’t think like you do, and really just listen. You can defend your thoughts another day. Today just try to learn.

item.title: Jasper County authorities warn businesses after reports of counterfeit $100 bills in Bay Springs - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
BAY SPRINGS – The Jasper County Sheriff’s Department is warning local businesses to be on alert after receiving reports of someone trying to pass counterfeit $100 bills at restaurants in Bay Springs.

In a social media post, the sheriff’s department said it received two reports Tuesday night involving attempts to use fake $100 bills at local restaurants.

Authorities urged merchants to use caution and watch for suspicious currency.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Jasper County Sheriff’s Department or the Bay Springs Police Department.

item.title: Hinds County sheriff says office will aggressively target gun conversion devices - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
HINDS COUNTY – The Hinds County Sheriff’s Office says it is continuing to prioritize gun violence and the illegal possession of machine gun conversion devices, commonly known as “switches.”

In a statement, Sheriff Tyree Jones said gun violence remains a threat to the safety of local communities and warned that conversion devices make firearms significantly more dangerous by turning them into fully automatic weapons.

Jones said the devices pose a serious risk to both the public and law enforcement and that anyone found in possession of them will face state and federal charges.

“The possession and use of these devices will continue to be aggressively prioritized by our deputies and investigative teams,” Jones said. “There is zero tolerance for them in Hinds County.”

The sheriff said deputies recovered a firearm equipped with a conversion device during a traffic stop the night before and arrested the person involved on multiple charges. No additional details about the arrest were immediately released.

Jones said the case reflects the ongoing efforts of the sheriff’s office to remove illegal weapons from the streets and hold offenders accountable.

The sheriff’s office said it will continue working to combat gun violence and protect residents across Hinds County.

item.title: AG Lynn Fitch and Coalition of AGs Support Rule to Hold PBMs Accountable - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON – Today, Attorney General Lynn Fitch joined a bipartisan coalition of 45 attorneys general in submitting a comment letter supporting a proposed U.S. Department of Labor (Department) rule that would require greater transparency from pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) that service employer-funded health plans covered under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA).

“PBMs have taken from the health care economy for far too long without giving back,” said Attorney General Lynn Fitch. “It is past time that there is accountability and an increase in transparency. I am proud to join my colleagues as we stand with consumers and community health providers to prevent PBMs from taking advantage of Mississippians.”

Approximately 136 million Americans receive health coverage through an employer — either their own job or a family member’s — and the proposed rule responds to concerns that employers often lack visibility into how PBMs are making money or why drug costs change. It would require PBMs to disclose twice a year how they generate revenue and would give employers the right to audit them. PBMs have also long sought to avoid state regulation by claiming federal preemption under ERISA. The attorneys general urge the Department to clarify that the proposed rule does not preempt state PBM transparency laws.

In the letter, the attorneys general ask the Department to further clarify that it supports working with them to enforce the rule. The AGs suggest language explicitly recognizing, “that state attorneys general play an important role in overseeing pharmacy benefit manager practices under applicable state law. Nothing in this rule is intended to preclude the Department from consulting, coordinating, sharing information as permitted by law, or referring matters to state attorneys general where the Department determines that state laws may be violated or that such cooperation would promote effective oversight and enforcement. Nor is this rule intended to displace or limit otherwise applicable, non-preempted state-law authority.”

Today, the top three PBMs manage approximately 80% of prescription drug claims. Due to the power imbalance held by PBMs and the negative effects of such power on drug pricing, all fifty states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico have enacted laws to rein them in. Attorney General Fitch has long worked to hold PBMs accountable for the role they play in inflating health care costs. For example, the $55.5-million settlement she negotiated in 2021 with Centene, required it to “provide full transparency related to the adjudication and payment of all pharmacy benefit claims.” That same year, she filed suit against the three largest PBMS for their role in the Insulin Pricing Scheme that has driven up the price of insulin by over 1,000 percent, even as the cost to produce it has actually decreased. In 2024, AG Fitch sued the PBMs for their role in the opioid epidemic. Just last year, she sued to enforce Mississippi law to give community pharmacists back leverage in negotiating drug reimbursement costs.

In submitting today’s comment letter, Attorney General Fitch joins the attorneys general of Alaska, American Samoa, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, and Wyoming.

You can read the letter here .

item.title: South Jackson parade set for Saturday with festivities at Cordoza Middle - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — The Association of South Jackson Neighborhoods will host its Annual South JXN Parade on Saturday, April 18, with activities beginning at 9 a.m. along McDowell Road.

The parade will start at the Little Caesars parking lot and travel to Cordoza Middle School, where organizers will hold additional festivities, including a fun zone for attendees.

Vendor setup is scheduled to begin at 7 a.m. at Cordoza Middle School, located at 3180 McDowell Road Extension, which will serve as the central hub for post-parade activities. City Council members Lashia Brown-Thomas and Kevin Parkinson are expected to attend and will be available for comment during the event.

Organizers said the annual parade is intended to bring together residents and celebrate the South Jackson community.

For more information, contact Ernest Ward at 601-201-3020 or Johnny Byrd at 601-720-9965.

item.title: Rankin County authorities investigate reports of trespassing near Reservoir neighborhood - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
RANKIN COUNTY – The Rankin County Sheriff’s Department said deputies searched a wooded area near the Bellegrove subdivision by the Reservoir after receiving a complaint about multiple unhoused individuals allegedly trespassing there, but no one was found.

According to the sheriff’s department, a complainant reported multiple unhoused individuals in the forested area adjacent to the neighborhood. During a preliminary investigation, deputies also found multiple online reports related to the matter, but authorities said no definitive location was identified.

The sheriff’s department said multiple deputies and long-range surveillance assets were deployed to search the area.

At the end of the search, deputies were unable to locate anyone in the wooded area adjacent to the subdivision, authorities said.

During the overland search, deputies noted that multiple homes bordering the wooded area were vacant. However, authorities said deputies were unable to establish cause to search those residences.

Anyone with information related to the incident or a more specific location is asked to contact the Rankin County Sheriff’s Department at 601-825-1480.

item.title: Philadelphia Teen Reported Missing After Last Seen in Meridian - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Digio Strategies
item.description:
Written by: Mackenzie Joiner

MERIDIAN – Authorities are asking for the public’s help in locating a missing juvenile reported as a runaway.

According to Philadelphia Police Chief Eric Lyons, 15-year-old Joleen Catherine Hatten of Philadelphia has been reported missing. She is described as 5 feet 4 inches tall and weighs approximately 125 pounds.

Hatten was last seen on April 13, 2026, along Highway 39 North in Meridian, Mississippi. At the time, she was wearing a yellow Lululemon sweater, black pants, and tan shoes.

Law enforcement officials urge anyone with information about her whereabouts to come forward immediately.

If you have any information, please contact the Meridian Police Department at 601-485-1893 or the Philadelphia Police Department at 601-656-2131.

Authorities remind the public that timely information can be critical in cases involving missing juveniles.

item.title: Passenger dies after motorcycle, car collide on U.S. 49 in Covington County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
COVINGTON COUNTY – A Moselle woman died after a crash involving a motorcycle and a passenger car Wednesday night on U.S. Highway 49 in Covington County, according to the Mississippi Highway Patrol.

The crash happened at about 9:55 p.m. April 15.

Troopers said a 2025 Kia K4 driven by 28-year-old April N. Clark of Taylorsville was traveling north on U.S. Highway 49 when it collided with a 2025 Kawasaki Ninja motorcycle also heading north.

The motorcycle was operated by 39-year-old James K. Morgan of Hattiesburg, according to MHP. A passenger on the motorcycle, 42-year-old Jennifer L. Bush of Moselle, was also involved in the crash.

Clark was taken by ambulance to a local hospital with serious injuries, troopers said. Morgan was also taken to a local hospital with serious injuries.

Bush was transported by ambulance to a local hospital with life-threatening injuries and later died, according to MHP.

The crash remains under investigation by the Mississippi Highway Patrol.

item.title: Parchman celebrates MS Rehabilitation Initiative graduation - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
Graduates of the inaugural commencement of the Mississippi Rehabilitation Initiative (MRI) at the Mississippi State Penitentiary were reminded to continue improving.

“Let this not be an end, but a starting point for your next phase of improvement and greatness,” said MRI Program Coordinator Teela Rivera in closing remarks last week.

The ceremony at the Chapel at Unit 30 was marked by emotional testimony from among the 37 graduates, including Inmates Willie Malone, Mekel Crumbly, Javari Harris, and David Weatherspoon.

Malone, 42, compared himself to a “broken crayon that still colors.”

Crumbly, 28, reflected on the mental shift required for success, noting that many had entered with a survival mindset rooted in past mistakes.

item.title: Mississippi Man Convicted in Louisiana Child Solicitation Case - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
COVINGTON, Louisiana — A Pearl River County connection played a role in the conviction of a Mississippi man found guilty of attempting to solicit a minor in St. Tammany Parish, authorities said.

Michael Stanley Lang, 56, of Poplarville, was convicted by a St. Tammany Parish jury of computer-aided solicitation of a minor following a trial presided over by Judge Richard Swartz.

Prosecutors said the case stemmed from an undercover investigation into online predators, with assistance from multiple agencies, including the Pearl River County Sheriff’s Office. Authorities said Lang engaged in explicit online conversations with someone he believed to be a 15-year-old girl, who was actually an undercover officer.

The investigation was initiated by the Covington Police Department and later involved several agencies, including the Slidell Police Department, Washington Parish Sheriff’s Office and Homeland Security Investigations.

During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence showing a pattern of sexually explicit communication and argued that Lang knowingly attempted to entice a minor. Assistant District Attorneys Christina Fisher and Taylor Nicholson said the defendant’s own statements helped establish his intent.

“The sexual conduct we discussed hits right on the head,” Nicholson told jurors during closing arguments. “Intent…how can we tell? His actions and words.”

Fisher added that Lang was fully aware of the age of the person he believed he was communicating with. “He knowingly communicated with a person who he reasonably believed was under 17,” she said. “Every piece of evidence points to his guilt.”

District Attorney Collin Sims said the conviction underscores the importance of protecting children from online predators.

“This conviction is a testament to the vigilance of our law enforcement partners and the skill of our prosecutors,” Sims said. “We will not allow those who target the vulnerable to hide behind a screen.” Lang was taken into custody following the verdict and booked into the St. Tammany Parish Sheriff’s Office. He is scheduled to be sentenced July 8 before Judge Swartz.

item.title: Mississippi drivers are at tipping point as gas costs strain daily life, survey finds - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
JACKSON — Mississippi drivers may still be about 80 cents away from their stated breaking point at the pump according to a recent study, but many middle-class residents say rising gas prices are already cutting into their quality of life and forcing difficult financial trade-offs.

A new survey from Advance America found Mississippi drivers would begin cutting back on essentials when gas reaches $4.56 per gallon. As of April 7, prices averaged $3.76, leaving what appears to be a cushion — but one that many households say feels increasingly thin as prices climb back above $4 nationally for the first time in four years.

Across the country, the study of 3,002 drivers highlights a growing sense of financial strain, with many Americans saying higher fuel costs are already reshaping spending habits before reaching their stated limits.

In Mississippi, lifestyle expenses are often the first to go. About 41% of respondents said they would cut back on dining out or takeout, while 29% pointed to travel and leisure. Still, some reported more concerning trade-offs: 13% said they would reduce grocery spending, and 3% said they would cut back on healthcare or medications.

Residents are also making day-to-day adjustments to cope with rising prices. About 40% said they would drive less, while 19% would combine trips or plan routes more carefully. Another 17% said they would take on extra work or find side income. Fewer respondents said they would consider more disruptive changes, such as switching to public transportation (8%), carpooling (7%) or changing jobs to shorten commutes (5%).

Despite those efforts, financial pressure is mounting. Nearly half of respondents — 49% — said they feel extremely or very stressed about fuel costs, while another 33% reported moderate stress. More than one-third, 37%, said rising gas prices have forced them to rely on credit or borrowing, and 43% said they have canceled plans with friends or family due to fuel costs.

“Gas prices don’t just hit wallets — they change behavior,” said Laura McCutcheon, vice president of marketing at Advance America. “What’s striking here is how little headroom many Americans feel they have left.”

Nationally, the survey found wide variation in how close drivers are to their financial tipping points. Vermont residents reported the narrowest margin, saying they would begin cutting back at $4.28 per gallon — just 17 cents above current prices there. In contrast, Alaska drivers reported the highest tolerance, with a threshold of $6.02 per gallon, or $1.40 above current prices.

While Mississippi is not yet at that tipping point on paper, the survey suggests many residents are already making sacrifices — a sign that the real impact of rising gas prices is being felt well before the numbers say it should.

item.title: MBI investigates fatal officer-involved shooting after alleged explosion attempt in Pascagoula - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
PASCAGOULA – The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation is investigating an officer-involved shooting involving the Jackson County Sheriff’s Office and Gautier Police Department that happened April 16 near Magnolia Street in Pascagoula.

According to MBI, the incident happened at about 12:20 p.m.

Investigators said the subject allegedly drove a vehicle through a fence and parked near a large propane tank. Authorities said the subject then tried to ignite propane tanks in the back of the vehicle in an apparent attempt to cause an explosion.

When law enforcement officers arrived, the subject ran from the scene, leading to a brief pursuit, MBI said.

During the pursuit, an exchange of gunfire occurred between the subject and law enforcement, according to investigators. The subject was fatally injured. No officers or deputies suffered any serious physical injuries.

MBI said the FBI and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives are also involved in the investigation.

The bureau said it is continuing to assess the incident and gather evidence. Once the investigation is complete, agents will turn over their findings to the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office.

MBI said the information released so far is preliminary and subject to change. Additional information may be released later.

item.title: Man charged after allegedly setting fire at grandmother’s home in Jackson - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – A Jackson man is facing arson-related charges after allegedly setting fire to grass in his grandmother’s yard and pouring gasoline in the driveway and carport of her home Friday, according to Fire Chief Charles Felton.

The incident happened March 27 at 5:35 p.m. at a home in the 500 block of Wellington Road in Jackson, Felton said.

Felton said Kahari Thicken ignited grass in the yard of his grandmother’s home. He also allegedly poured gasoline in the driveway and carport area but did not ignite it.

Thicken, who is from Jackson, will be charged with third-degree arson involving personal property and fourth-degree arson for attempted arson, Felton said.

No additional information was immediately available.

item.title: LeFleur’s Bluff Playground Ranked Among Nation’s Best in USA TODAY 10BEST Awards - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
JACKSON – The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks is proud to announce that LeFleur’s Bluff Playground has been named a top public playground in the nation, earning 6th place in the USA TODAY 10BEST Readers’ Choice Awards for Best Public Playground.

Located within the LeFleur’s Bluff Complex (LBC) in Jackson, the playground sits on a shared campus with the Mississippi Museum of Natural Science and the Mississippi Children’s Museum.

The 30,000-square-foot, state-of-the-art playground was designed with accessibility and outdoor exploration in mind featuring more than 80 play elements, 73 of which are inclusive for children with accessibility needs. The playground is divided into age-appropriate areas for children ages 6 months to 12 years old and encourages active play through climbing, running, and exploration.

In addition to its innovative design, the playground includes shade structures that cover approximately 75 percent of the area, helping reduce temperatures by up to 30 degrees and allowing for more comfortable, year-round use. Admission to the park is free and open to the public.

“This recognition is a testament to the power of creating spaces where every child can play, explore, and feel included,” said Angel Rohnke, Director of the Mississippi Museum of Natural Science. “LeFleur’s Bluff Playground was designed to welcome families of all abilities, and we’re honored to see it recognized among the best in the country.”

“LeFleur’s Bluff Playground has become more than a place to play, it’s a place where our community comes together,” said Emily Hoff, Executive Director of the Mississippi Children’s Museum. “From neighborhood families to visitors discovering Jackson for the first time, this park is a welcoming beacon in Mississippi’s capital city, inviting children of every age and ability to explore, connect, and make memories together.”

The Blue Cross & Blue Shield of Mississippi Foundation’s generous $4.2 million grant for improving the health and well-being of Mississippians made this innovative project possible and their leadership team played a visionary role in the LBC’s development.

To learn more about LeFleur’s Bluff Playground and The Mississippi Museum of Natural Science visit https://www.mdwfp.com/museum-natural-science/lefleurs-bluff-playground .

item.title: Keynote at Community Work Center was Homecoming for Estes - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
FLOWOOD – The graduation of the latest alcohol and drug program at the Community Work Center in Flowood was a homecoming for keynote speaker Courtney Estes.

Estes agreed to return to help inspire and motivate the current inmates to keep working through their recovery. She is now preparing to be ordained as a minister next month, giving credit to the Flowood facility for helping her recovery.

Just eight years ago, Estes was an inmate at the Flowood facility following a conviction for possession of methamphetamine. She decided to change and worked toward that change until her release in December 2024.

“Eight years ago, I was right where you are now. I lived in Room 3 right over there,” she said, pointing behind her. “I am blessed to come back to pour into these women the knowledge and show them they are not alone. They can be successful, and they can be a light to others.”

Program leader George Schmaus said the Flowood program is the only A&D program in the prison system that uses peer facilitators to help inmates through the course.

“It is not a small thing to graduate from A&D,” Schmaus said, noting that the class started with 21 inmates. “This is a really big accomplishment, and we have a wonderful team of peer facilitators who work with the participants.”

A class of 13 women celebrated completing the 25-week rehabilitation program. The women are incarcerated mostly on drug convictions.

Among the graduates were Melissa Ann Buse and Emily Stuart.

Buse said the program helped her focus on the root cause of her addiction and its effect on her family.

Stuart said it made her realize she had been wrong about whether it was relevant to her. “I never realized how serious my addictions were until I started recovery,” Buse said.

Being involved in drugs for about 40 years, Buse said, “I have a long way to go, but I am on my way.” The 59-year-old is serving a 20-year sentence for possession of a controlled substance in Stone County.

Stuart, who is serving a 10-year sentence for identity theft, said she did not fall into the typical drug stereotype, but drugs still inflicted devastation in her life.

“I enrolled feeling like an outsider. I had never used drugs, so I thought this program was not relevant. I was wrong. I was not a user, but I was a by-product of it,” Stuart said. “I was with others who were addicted, and I made poor decisions. I was angry and destructive. I was hurt, and what does a hurt person do? They hurt others.”

The women can change, as evidenced by Estes. Estes described how she started her decline through methamphetamine, and by age 18, she was using almost all kinds of other drugs.

She became pregnant, divorced, and continued with abusive relationships. She was eventually arrested and convicted of possession of meth with intent to distribute.

“I really don’t know how I even got here because I came in the door high. The Lord paved the way for me,” Estes said.

While at the Flowood CWC, Estes said she made a life-changing decision.

“I was sick and tired of being sick and tired. I was not going to leave the way I came in,” she said, describing the changes made in her attitude and mindset. “I started being compliant. I started doing my programs. I started taking my sobriety and recovery seriously.”

Finishing her new mission was a major milestone for Estes.

“Whenever I graduated A&D, that was the first thing I had ever graduated from in my entire life. I had a GED, but I had not gotten a diploma. I had never shaken someone’s hand to accept a diploma for anything. That fire boosted me,” Estes said, describing how she began rebuilding her life, reestablishing connections with family, and finding her career after her release.

item.title: Joint narcotics investigation in Laurel leads to 2 arrests, drug and firearm seizures - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JONES COUNTY – A joint narcotics investigation by the Laurel Police Department and the Jones County Sheriff’s Department led to multiple arrests Wednesday and the seizure of illegal drugs, a firearm and cash.

According to Laurel police, the department’s Narcotic Division and Jones County sheriff’s narcotics investigators carried out the investigation April 15.

As part of the operation, officers executed a search warrant in the 1500 block of North 3rd Avenue in Laurel. Investigators said they found about 2 grams of cocaine, 12 grams of marijuana, a firearm and an undisclosed amount of U.S. currency.

Jonas Windham was arrested and charged with ex-convict in possession of a weapon and possession of a controlled substance, police said.

In a related operation, Laurel police conducted a traffic stop near U.S. Highway 84 West and 16th Avenue based on information gathered through the joint investigation, authorities said. During the stop, officers found about 56 grams of methamphetamine, according to police.

Patrick Anderson was arrested and charged with possession of a controlled substance with intent to distribute.

Police said the arrests and seizures are part of an ongoing collaborative investigation that began with warrants and arrests earlier this week by the Jones County Sheriff’s Department in Ellisville.

“The success of this operation stemmed from our departments working together,” Sgt. Michelle Howell of the Laurel Police Department said. “We look forward to continued collaboration on future investigations. Both departments are dedicated to ridding the community of illegal narcotics.”

The investigation remains ongoing, and additional arrests or charges may follow.

item.title: Horhn defends police chief contract, cites potential private funding option - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Jackson Mayor John Horhn is defending the contract for Police Chief Dr. RaShall Brackney, calling her “among the best in the business” while acknowledging concerns from the City Council amid a budget shortfall.

In a statement released this week, Horhn said the city must be willing to offer competitive incentives to attract top law enforcement leadership.

“Jackson needs the best in the business to lead crime-fighting here, and I believe that Chief Brackney is among the best in the business,” Horhn said. “When you have the opportunity to grab talent like that, you often have to incentivize them to take the job.”

The mayor said his administration is aware of the council’s concerns about the cost of the contract and the city’s financial constraints. He noted that officials have already made the council aware of the budget shortfall.

To address the issue, Horhn said the city is exploring a philanthropic funding option to help meet the terms of Brackney’s agreement. Details of that arrangement are still being worked out, he said.

Horhn emphasized that his goal is to resolve the matter in a way that is financially responsible and in the city’s best interest.

He added that his administration has consistently relied on partnerships beyond city government to fund key initiatives, pointing to collaborations with corporate, nonprofit and philanthropic groups on infrastructure, cultural events, and public safety efforts.

“We have been focused on finding creative and responsible ways to fund our vision for Jackson,” Horhn said. “Public-private partnerships have been a defining feature of this Administration from day one.”

The mayor said that approach will continue as the city works to balance its financial challenges with efforts to strengthen public safety.

item.title: What to know about Asian needle ants as Mississippi tracks invasive species - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
The Mississippi State University Extension Service is urging residents to learn more about the invasive Asian needle ant, a species that has been found in the state and can pose both health and ecological concerns.

According to MSU Extension, the Asian needle ant, known scientifically as Brachyponera chinensis , was first reported in Mississippi in 2013. The ants are small, about one-fifth of an inch long, dark brown to black, shiny and have a single large node on their waist, known as the petiole.

Extension officials said that, aside from a single confirmed colony in Lowndes County in 2025, other findings in Mississippi have been isolated.

The ants are not considered aggressive and will usually avoid people when possible, according to MSU Extension. Most stings happen accidentally. Like many ant species, the Asian needle ant uses a stinger to inject venom, which can cause a painful defensive sting.

MSU Extension said the ant’s venom has been linked to life-threatening allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, though such reactions are not especially common. Officials said people who are allergic to stings from other insects should be aware that they could also experience a severe reaction from these ants.

The ants are usually found outdoors in wooded areas, often nesting under leaf litter, pine needles and rotting logs.

Researchers said the species can build large populations that outcompete, displace or prey on other insects, creating a significant ecological concern in areas where infestations become established. MSU researchers said they are continuing to track the spread of the ants and monitor infested sites to study effects on native species and local ecosystems.

To help reduce possible harborage areas, Extension officials recommend moving firewood piles away from homes and removing piles of leaves or pine needles.

Residents who believe they have seen Asian needle ants are encouraged to submit physical specimens and collection information to the MSU Extension Insect ID Lab to help researchers track the species’ spread in Mississippi.

item.title: MISSING IN MISSISSIPPI: Blair Ivy, Clarke County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
QUITMAN — The disappearance of Alisha “Blair” Ivy remains one of Clarke County’s most haunting unsolved cases, with investigators and family still searching for answers more than seven years later in what authorities believe is a case of foul play.

Ivy, 23 at the time, was last seen Oct. 28, 2018, at a residence on Long Boulevard in Quitman. She is a white female with dark brown hair, green eyes, 5’11” tall and about 175 pounds, with several tattoos on her upper leg, chest, back and arms.

According to investigators, Ivy had been staying with a male friend, Steve Ray Perry, at the time of her disappearance. A close friend visited her the day she was last seen. Before the friend left, Ivy said her ex-boyfriend was on the way and that she would make contact later.

She never did.

When first questioned, Perry told authorities he had not seen Ivy that day. After investigators obtained surveillance footage from a neighboring home showing Ivy at the residence, he changed his account, saying Ivy told him she was going to meet her ex-boyfriend before leaving through the back door.

It remains unclear whether Ivy ever met up with her ex. Investigators say her cellphone was active later that afternoon, sending a text message around 4:07 p.m. from an area near the southwestern part of Clarke County and the Jasper County line. Her phone pinged off the Voss tower, which covers a roughly 25-mile radius including parts of Clarke, Jasper and Jones County.

Family members say Ivy’s sudden disappearance was out of character, noting she rarely went more than a day without contacting loved ones. Concern grew almost immediately when she failed to reach out.

Her father, Ferlin Ivy, has described the years since as a painful, ongoing ordeal, recalling the last time he saw his daughter on the day before she disappeared.

“She brought me a plate lunch and she was telling me how much she loves me,” he told WTOK in an interview in 2019.

Authorities with the Clarke County Sheriff’s Department have conducted multiple searches and canvasses with the help of volunteers, but leads have slowed over time. Former Sheriff Todd Kemp said during the years surrounding the early investigation that evidence uncovered in the case points to foul play.

“We feel something bad has happened, no doubt, but what and who did it, we still don’t know,” Kemp said, urging anyone with information, no matter how small, to come forward.

Despite the years that have passed, Ivy’s family continues to hold onto hope that answers will come.

“Blair, if you’re out there, I hope you’re safe,” her father said in the interview with WTOK. “I love you and I want you to come home.”

Anyone with information about Ivy’s disappearance is urged to contact the Clarke County Sheriff’s Department at 601-776-5252 or East Mississippi Crime Stoppers at 855-485-TIPS.

Family members say Ivy’s sudden disappearance was out of character, noting she rarely went more than a day without contacting loved ones. Concern grew almost immediately when she failed to reach out.

Her father, Ferlin Ivy, has described the years since as a painful, ongoing ordeal, recalling the last time he saw his daughter on the day before she disappeared.

“She brought me a plate lunch and she was telling me how much she loves me,” he told WTOK in an interview in 2019.

Authorities with the Clarke County Sheriff’s Department have conducted multiple searches and canvasses with the help of volunteers, but leads have slowed over time. Former Sheriff Todd Kemp said during the years surrounding the early investigation that evidence uncovered in the case points to foul play.

“We feel something bad has happened, no doubt, but what and who did it, we still don’t know,” Kemp said, urging anyone with information, no matter how small, to come forward.

Despite the years that have passed, Ivy’s family continues to hold onto hope that answers will come.

“Blair, if you’re out there, I hope you’re safe,” her father said in the interview with WTOK. “I love you and I want you to come home.”

Anyone with information about Ivy’s disappearance is urged to contact the Clarke County Sheriff’s Department at 601-776-5252 or East Mississippi Crime Stoppers at 855-485-TIPS.

item.title: MC students present original discoveries during Research Week 2026 - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
By Bruce Coleman Mississippi College

CLINTON – Undergraduate and graduate students from a wide range of academic disciplines at Mississippi College will share their original research during Research Week 2026, scheduled from April 21 to 24 on the Clinton campus.

Christian Pinnen, MC professor of history and political science, said about 130 MC students will present posters and papers describing projects originating from the MC Departments of Biological Sciences, Chemistry and Biochemistry, Electrical Engineering, English and Philosophy, History and Political Science, Psychology and Social Work, Public Health, and the Schools of Nursing and Science and Mathematics.

“Research Week 2026 shows that Mississippi College students, under our faculty’s expert guidance, are producing some excellent research,” said Pinnen, who coordinates MC’s Research Week Committee. “It also showcases the overall academic quality of the research programs we have at MC.”

He said the event highlights notable student projects and fosters collaboration between academic disciplines across campus.

One study that indicates how MC students contribute to the University’s discovery enterprise is a project that centers on the stars and nebulae in the Orion constellation.

Inspired by a presentation from a NASA staff member last fall and made possible by the donation of a large telescope to MC’s Chemistry and Biochemistry Department by Tammy Jan Sander of Madison, the study employed spectral analysis to determine the chemical composition of certain starlight and nebulae.

“Each chemical element leaves a unique spectral fingerprint,” explained Scoty Hearst, assistant professor in the MC Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry and coordinator of the study. “By using spectral analysis of images taken with our telescopes using special spectral filters, we can determine which elements are present.”

He said MC students have analyzed the chemical composition of stars in the Orion constellation, the Orion Nebula, the Running Man nebula, the Horse Head Nebula and the Monkey Head Nebula.

“Star spectroscopy is a branch of astrophysics, but it’s based on chemical principles,” Hearst said. “We have incorporated these techniques into our classes, where students perform star spectroscopy and use their data to write lab reports.

“Research is important for preparing students for future careers in STEM fields, and for developing critical-thinking skills needed in graduate school. This research has inspired students to explore the universe and to observe what is above their heads.”

Similarly, Pinnen said Research Week encourages more students to become involved in research.

“This event helps give them an idea about the academic process and what it takes to present original research at an actual conference,” he said. “When people ask them questions about their work, they gain new perspectives. That’s very much a part of academic tradition at a liberal arts institution, and it’s how they learn.

“They dig into a topic, do their research, and defend their conclusions. That exposes them to the full gamut of the academic experience.”

Research Week 2026 will begin at 9:30 a.m. on Tuesday, April 21, when undergraduate students will give presentations on biology research during “Introduction to Biological Data Analysis,” in room 201 of the Hederman Science Building.

Paper and poster presentations will take place on Wednesday, April 22. History panels are scheduled from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. in Meeting Room A in the B.C. Rogers Student Center, while interdisciplinary inquiry panels are scheduled from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. in Meeting Rooms A and B in the B.C. Rogers Student Center.

That afternoon, poster presentations in psychology (from 1 to 2 p.m.), biology and nursing (from 2 to 3 p.m.), as well as chemistry and biochemistry, and English (from 3 to 4 p.m.) will be displayed in Anderson Hall in B.C. Rogers.

Research Week 2026 will wrap up with presentations by senior students in MC’s Department of Electrical Engineering at 1:30 p.m. on Friday, April 24, in room 306 of the Hederman Science Building.

All Research Week events are free and open to the public. For more information, visit https://www.mc.edu/academics/research-week .

item.title: Marshall County Correctional Facility Celebrates Graduates Focused on Rehabilitation and Re-Entry - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
HOLLY SPRINGS — The Marshall County Correctional Facility is celebrating a new class of graduates from the Mississippi Rehabilitative Initiative, a program aimed at helping incarcerated individuals adopt healthier behaviors and prepare for re-entry into society.

The graduation ceremony, held April 7, marked the completion of an approximately nine-month, evidence-based program that includes education, behavioral therapy and job training components.

Participants in the Mississippi Rehabilitative Initiative, also known as MRI, completed coursework such as GED or HiSet preparation, Moral Reconation Therapy, Thinking for a Change, a 100-hour re-entry program, and vocational career training. The program also includes classes in criminological and sociological theory, substance abuse education and other electives designed to support long-term behavioral change.

Superintendent Frank Caswell said the graduates demonstrated discipline and commitment throughout the program.

“This represents more than certificates — it represents second chances, accountability, and a new direction,” Caswell said. “Each graduate made a decision to invest in themselves, and that decision will impact not only their future but also their families and communities.”

Caswell encouraged participants to remain focused on their goals and continue making positive choices, emphasizing that their past does not define their future.

item.title: George County deputies search for runaway 15-year-old last believed to be in Biloxi - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
GEORGE COUNTY – The George County Sheriff’s Office is asking for the public’s help in locating a runaway 15-year-old who may be in Biloxi.

Authorities identified the teen as Kaelynn Underwood.

According to the sheriff’s office, Kaelynn is about 4 feet 10 inches tall, weighs about 100 pounds and recently dyed her hair black.

Investigators said she was last seen at her residence on Marshall Smith Road. The sheriff’s office said Kaelynn was first reported as a runaway on March 8, 2026, and was later located. She has since been reported missing again after running away April 14.

Authorities said investigators have received information indicating she may be in the city of Biloxi.

Anyone with information about Kaelynn’s whereabouts is asked to contact the George County Sheriff’s Office at 601-947-9156 or their local law enforcement agency.

Anonymous tips may also be submitted through Mississippi Coast Crime Stoppers by calling 877-787-5898, visiting mscoastcrimestoppers.com, or through the sheriff’s office website.

item.title: Bicyclist Killed in Early Morning Crash on Highway 611 in Jackson County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON COUNTY — A bicyclist was killed in a three-vehicle crash early Sunday on Highway 611 in Jackson County, according to the Mississippi Highway Patrol.

The crash occurred around 5 a.m. when a 2008 Honda Accord driven by Dilaila Ortiz, 22, of Gautier, and a 2016 Toyota Camry driven by James Baxter, 39, were traveling north on Highway 611 and collided with a bicyclist.

Authorities identified the bicyclist as Temario Compton, 35, of Mobile. He sustained fatal injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene.

Officials said neither Ortiz nor Baxter was injured in the crash.

The cause of the crash remains under investigation by the Mississippi Highway Patrol.

item.title: VA medical center to host veterans food pantry in Jackson on April 18 - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – The G.V. (Sonny) Montgomery VA Medical Center will host its monthly Veterans Food Pantry on Saturday, April 18, 2026, at its main campus in Jackson.

The drive-thru event is scheduled from 9 a.m. to 11 a.m. at the front entrance of the medical center.

According to the VA medical center, the pantry will provide perishable and nonperishable food to veterans experiencing food insecurity.

The event is being led by the Center for Development and Civic Engagement, formerly known as Voluntary Service.

More information is available through the G.V. (Sonny) Montgomery VA Medical Center.
